en.title: The FX Exposure Nobody Put in the AI Budget
en.titleCore: FX exposure on AI vendor bills
en.description: AI spend is invoiced in USD, consumed in local teams, and budgeted annually. The currency line is a variance driver nobody modelled.
en.body:
AI vendor spend has three currencies in it and only one of them is the token rate. Invoices arrive in US dollars, teams that generate the consumption are frequently elsewhere, and the budget is typically set annually. That combination creates a variance driver that does not appear in any token dashboard, and it lands directly in the forecast-versus-actual line.

Where the exposure actually sits

  • Invoice currency vs reporting currency. A USD invoice against a EUR or BRL reporting entity is a translation exposure, not a hedging decision, and it belongs in the variance bridge.
  • Local team spend, USD budget. The consumption is generated by a distributed team but the budget is a single number. Without a per-team cost allocation, an FX move and a usage move are indistinguishable in the actuals.
  • The annual-budget mismatch. A rate move inside the budget year changes the run-rate without any change in usage. That is the hardest kind of variance to explain to a board, because nothing operational changed.

Three controls that take an afternoon

  1. Split the variance bridge into price, usage and FX. If those three are not separated, a currency move gets reported as a usage problem and the team is sent to optimise something that is not broken.
  2. Hold the token rate and the invoice currency apart in the model. They move independently and only one of them is negotiable by your optimisation work.
  3. Carry a sensitivity, not a point estimate. A budget that assumes a single FX rate is a budget with an unhedged assumption in it. A stated sensitivity is defensible; a silent one is not.

What to tell the board

The honest framing is that a portion of AI spend variance is not operational. Give the board the FX-only line, separate from the usage and price lines, so the operational team is only measured on what it controls. It also creates a cheap strategic lever: a forecast of how much spend a hedge or a settlement-currency change would save is a number nobody has asked for yet.

Bottom line

Token price is the cost everyone forecasts. Currency is the cost everyone discovers in month-end. Split price, usage and FX in the variance bridge, and a quarter of unexplained variance usually stops being unexplained.

faq.question: Why does AI spend have foreign exchange exposure?
faq.answer: Because the invoice currency, the team generating the consumption and the reporting currency are frequently three different things. A USD invoice against a non-USD reporting entity is a translation exposure that moves run-rate with no change in usage.

faq.question: How do we separate FX from usage in our AI variance analysis?
faq.answer: Split the variance bridge into price, usage and FX as three independent lines. Without that split a currency move is reported as a usage problem and the operational team is asked to optimise something that is not broken.

faq.question: Should we hedge our AI vendor spend?
faq.answer: At minimum carry a stated sensitivity rather than a point estimate, so the budget assumption is visible. A forecast of what a hedge or a settlement-currency change would save is itself a useful number to bring to the board.
